title: Aid cuts are pushing Bangladesh's NGOs from services to lending
excerpt: A BIDS study finds the aid fall is permanent, 2,170 NGOs have no lending income, and many are cutting social services first and turning into lenders.

image.alt: A community health worker in Dhaka's Korail settlement holds a bag of family planning supplies
image.credit: DFID - UK Department for International Development / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0

content:
DEVLENS SPECIAL · Explanatory report · NGO financing · 13 November 2026

A new BIDS study finds that the fall in foreign aid is permanent, that 2,170 NGOs have no lending income to fall back on, and that many are cutting social services first and turning into lenders. It also finds the state would pay almost three times as much to deliver some of those services itself.

The short answer

On 6 October 2026, the Bangladesh Institute of Development Studies (BIDS) presented the most detailed study yet of what the global aid cuts mean for Bangladesh's NGOs. Its central finding is not only that NGOs are losing money. It is what they do when they lose it.

An NGO that loses a grant still has to pay rent, salaries and loan officers. If it also runs microfinance, the lending earns income and the social work does not. So the social work goes first: the health outreach, the legal aid, the school programme. Over time, the study warns, smaller NGOs turn into plain microfinance companies. BIDS calls this mission drift.

That matters because those services are not easy to replace. Using a new model, the BIDS team estimates that if the government tried to deliver services where NGOs have the advantage, such as community mental health, legal aid and finding the right people for safety-net programmes, it would cost about 2.9 times as much for each unit of service that actually works. A commercial company would cost about 6.4 times as much.

The researchers' conclusion is direct. Foreign aid will not come back, and no private source is large enough to replace it. Only the government has a budget of the right size: all foreign grants to NGOs together equal about 3.4% of one year's Annual Development Programme.

Inside the study

The study was led by Dr Kazi Iqbal, research director at BIDS, with Professor A K Enamul Haque, the institute's director general, Badrun Nessa Ahmed, Md Riaz Uddin and Kazi Zubair Hossain. It was presented at a seminar titled "Beyond Donor Dependence: The Future of NGO Financing in Bangladesh", with Finance and Planning Minister Amir Khosru Mahmud Chowdhury as chief guest.

The team used organisation-level data from the NGO Affairs Bureau and the Microcredit Regulatory Authority (MRA), and ran an online survey of 48 NGOs that also run microfinance, between June and September 2026. It also reviewed public procurement rules, the draft CSR and partnership policies, and international experience.

One point needs care. Several newspapers reported that the study surveyed 46 NGOs and found budget falls of 40% for grant-only NGOs and 12% for those with microfinance. Those figures do not appear in the presentation itself, which reports a survey of 48 NGO-MFIs and losses of roughly 30% among those hit. Devlens uses the presentation's figures.

Why the money is not coming back

Net official development assistance from rich countries fell by 19% in 2025, the largest annual contraction on record, BIDS found from OECD data. About $50 billion was lost between 2023 and 2025, and the OECD expects a further fall of 5.8% to 6.9% in 2026.

The cut was concentrated. Five donors accounted for 96% of it. US aid fell by 57%, Germany's by 17%, the UK's by 11%, France's by 10.9% and Japan's by 6%. The US did more than cut: it dismantled USAID, cancelling 83% of its programmes, along with the contracting systems and expertise that ran them.

The cuts also changed the kind of aid that is left. Bilateral grants were cut three times as hard as loans, by 29% against 10%. Humanitarian aid fell by 35.8%. Nutrition (-46.6%), food security (-38.3%) and water and sanitation (-38.1%) were hit hardest. Health was the only major sector that grew.

Why call this permanent rather than a bad patch, as in the 1990s? Because the cuts are written into budgets for years ahead, because money is moving to defence (NATO members have committed to spend 5% of GDP by 2035), and because the case for aid has changed. Donors increasingly tie aid to their own strategic interests rather than to need.

Who is exposed

As of August 2026, 2,804 active NGOs were registered with the NGO Affairs Bureau. Of these, 2,170 were what BIDS calls pure-service NGOs: registered to receive foreign money, but with no microcredit licence. That is about three in four. They have no lending surplus to fall back on, and they are the core of the roughly 2,200 NGOs that newspapers described as at risk.

The headline money does not yet show the damage. Foreign grants released through the bureau peaked at $955 million in FY2018-19, fell to $655 million at their low point, and recovered to $838 million in FY2025-26. But the money is being spread thinner. The average grant released per project fell from $725,000 in FY2014-15 to $507,000 in FY2025-26: more, smaller projects. For a small NGO, a smaller project means less room to cover the fixed costs that keep the organisation running.

The microfinance NGOs look safer, and as a group they are. Across the NGO-MFI sector, donor money is now just 0.19% of the fund base, which comes mostly from members' savings and retained surplus. But that average hides the small players. MFIs with loan books under Tk 50 crore still rely on donors for 11.6% to 14.6% of their funds.

How a funding cut becomes mission drift

In the BIDS survey, 70% of NGO-MFIs said they had been hit by fund cuts, and the affected organisations had lost roughly 30% of their budgets. International NGOs reported cuts of 20% to 50%.

Most responded the same way: they cut costs. Staff went, salaries were reduced, and projects were merged. Few had managed to start a social business or win replacement money from the government.

The sequence that follows is the study's most important finding. Grant income falls, but fixed costs stay. Social services earn nothing, so they are cut first. Lending earns service charges, so it stays. Step by step, a development organisation becomes a lender.

The researchers warn that this undermines the lending too. Microfinance in Bangladesh works because borrowers trust the organisation, and much of that trust was built through the health camps, schools and legal help that are now being cut.

The service cuts are already visible. Two partners of the International Planned Parenthood Federation (IPPF) show what happens to the people at the end of the chain. Bandhu Social Welfare Society lost two US-funded projects worth about $2 million, laid off 120 staff and closed 62% of its service points, affecting about 15,000 people receiving HIV prevention and treatment. Population Services and Training Center (PSTC) lost about 30% of its 2025 budget, ended 37 positions and expected to reach 11,000 fewer outreach clients. Both dropped rights and advocacy work first.

Why NGOs are worth paying for

The study asks a question the sector rarely answers with numbers: when should a service be run by the government, an NGO, a company, or a partnership?

Its answer starts from a simple idea: a service delivered is not a service that works. Between the two sit six leaks. A provider has to reach people, operate at scale, persuade people to take the service up, fit it to their needs, keep quality up where no one checks, and get the technical work right. Each kind of provider loses different amounts at each step. BIDS turns this into a model that weighs the value of the service that actually works against its cost.

The model's results match what already works in Bangladesh. Routine immunisation at fixed clinics is best left to the government. But reaching families who are reluctant to vaccinate works best as a partnership: the government supplies the vaccine, and an NGO persuades the family.

The cost of getting this wrong is large. Where NGOs have the advantage, as in community mental health, legal aid and identifying people for safety-net programmes, government delivery would cost about 2.9 times as much per unit of effective service, and a commercial firm about 6.4 times as much. Letting NGO services collapse is not a saving. It moves the cost somewhere more expensive.

Where replacement money could come from

BIDS looked at four domestic sources. Only one is big enough.

Government contracts. The government already works with NGOs through four channels: competitive contracts, memoranda of understanding, apex bodies such as PKSF, and community contracting. But contract values are never published. The Public Procurement Rules 2025 recognise service contracts and simplify requests for proposals, but they still require a 100% unconditional bank guarantee, which cash-poor NGOs cannot provide. A draft GO-NGO Partnership Policy 2026 would add joint action plans, a management information system, social audits and payment by results. The FY2026-27 budget also sets aside Tk 300 crore for the creative economy, with another Tk 500 crore expected from bank CSR, and NGOs such as Aarong and Caritas already link rural artisans to markets.

Corporate social responsibility (CSR). Bank CSR spending fell 69% between 2022 and 2025, to Tk 345 crore, and fell another 21% in the first half of 2026. It is pro-cyclical: it shrinks when banks struggle, which is exactly when need rises. A draft National CSR Policy 2026 would require covered companies to spend 1% of pre-tax profit and names NGOs as an implementing channel. But BIDS notes gaps: no central register of NGOs, so access depends on each company's judgement; no cap on companies' own foundations; and no penalty for not spending.

Social business. Bangladesh has no legal definition of a social business, no asset lock, no certification and no preference in procurement. The track record follows a clear logic. Social businesses that turn an existing asset or service into income tend to succeed: Aarong, the RDRS eye hospital, Sochetan schools. Ventures built from scratch that need heavy capital tend to fail: Grameen Danone and RDRS's feed mills struggled with cold-chain costs and management.

New forms of finance. Outcome-based finance, bonds and carbon credits need a steady stream of income to borrow against, which only large NGOs have. Bangladesh has some history here, including BRAC's microcredit securitisation in 2006 and SAJIDA Foundation's bonds in 2021 and 2026, but the market has shrunk. Diaspora giving is a possibility: remittances reached $30.32 billion, and 0.1% of that would be $30 million a year, but the systems for collecting it are weak.

The logic of the comparison points one way. CSR shrinks when the economy does, social business works only for some, and new finance suits only the largest NGOs. The government's development budget is the only pool large enough to replace foreign grants, and it already pays for services NGOs can deliver more cheaply.

What BIDS recommends

  1. Hire NGOs to implement government projects where they have the advantage.
  2. Create a dedicated fund or budget line for NGOs.
  3. Simplify NGO Affairs Bureau approvals and the release of funds.
  4. Give tax incentives for local giving and CSR, and route CSR money through registered NGOs.

The minister's response suggests the government is listening but not yet committed. "We are working without a policy," Amir Khosru Mahmud Chowdhury said at the seminar. He said no project would be approved unless it meets four tests: value for money, return on investment, jobs or new enterprises, and environmental protection. State Minister for Planning Zonayed Abdur Rahim Saki said guidelines on government-NGO relations were being finalised, and added that "the foreign financing of NGOs is almost coming to an end in view of LDC graduation".

What small NGOs can do now

  • Protect the services that build trust. The study's warning is that cutting them first weakens the organisation's whole base, including its lending.
  • Turn what you already have into income. The social businesses that worked converted an existing asset or service. Building a new venture from scratch rarely did.
  • Get ready for government contracts. Keep audited accounts current, document results, and prepare to show value for money under the minister's four tests. The draft partnership policy pays by results.
  • Work through apex bodies and consortia. PKSF works through 278 partner organisations and is an accredited national entity for the Adaptation Fund and the Green Climate Fund. Joining such channels lets small NGOs reach money they cannot apply for alone.

What to watch

  • The draft GO-NGO Partnership Policy 2026: whether it comes with a budget line, and whether the bank guarantee rule changes for NGOs.
  • The draft National CSR Policy 2026: whether it adds a central NGO register and consequences for not spending.
  • A legal definition of social business.
  • The OECD's 2026 aid figures, expected in April 2027, to see whether the further fall it projects comes true.
  • Bangladesh's LDC graduation in November 2029, which officials already cite as a reason foreign NGO funding will shrink.

About this analysis

This report draws on the presentation that BIDS researchers gave on 6 October 2026, "Beyond Donor Dependence: The Future of NGO Financing in Bangladesh", and on press coverage of the seminar. The full paper has not yet been published. Some newspapers reported a different survey size and different budget figures; where they differ, Devlens follows the presentation. The presentation dates the low point in grant releases, $655 million, to FY2021-22, but NGO Affairs Bureau data published by The Financial Express put it in FY2023-24, and this report uses the bureau's series. The estimate that about three in four NGOs have no lending income is a Devlens calculation from the BIDS figures. The examples of service cuts come from IPPF's reporting on its partners in Bangladesh. Graphics are by Devlens Bangladesh.
